reading.title: Interpreting named menu categories
reading.text: A hospitality trainee reads a fictional list of named mixed drinks. The first group is Martini, Old Fashioned, Manhattan and Negroni. Another group is Daiquiri, Margarita, Mojito and Whiskey Sour. The list then names Sidecar, Sazerac, Cosmopolitan and Piña Colada. Long Island Iced Tea, Moscow Mule and Gimlet complete the selection. These names refer to different customary categories; they are not descriptions of the glass alone. Long Island Iced Tea is usually alcoholic despite its tea-like name. Recipes and variants differ, so the trainee asks what the venue means and whether an alcohol-free alternative is available. The worksheet practices menu reading without giving quantities, preparation instructions, purchase recommendations or an assumption that the learner will consume any item.

reading.title: Separating names from preparation words
reading.text: The trainee compares Tom Collins, Paloma, Aperol Spritz, Espresso Martini and Dark and Stormy as named menu categories. The next words describe preparation rather than product identity. Shaken means mixed by shaking; stirred means mixed with a stirring tool. Muddled concerns pressing ingredients, layered concerns separate layers, and blended here means processed with a blender. Built means assembled in the serving glass. Strained means passed through a strainer, while double strained involves two strainers. Flamed describes a flame-related presentation technique rather than a direction to ignite anything. Infused concerns contact with an ingredient to extract flavor. The learner can explain these words without performing the techniques. The worksheet gives no flame, chemical or operational instructions and does not establish suitability from an image.

reading.title: Clarifying service expressions
reading.text: The trainee checks expressions before interpreting a request. On the rocks means served over ice. Neat means without ice or added mixers. Straight up generally means chilled with no ice remaining, but usage varies, so clarification can help. Dirty commonly concerns olive brine in a martini. Dry in this martini context usually indicates less vermouth, while wet indicates more; it is different from a wine's residual-sugar classification. Virgin commonly requests an alcohol-free version, whose actual ingredients still need checking. Top shelf describes a venue's premium range rather than guaranteed quality. Well drink uses its standard house spirit, and house special names a featured item. The learner practices clarifying terms without making, recommending or consuming a beverage and without treating a menu phrase as a chemical certification.
